Chapter 3: The Myth of Neutrality and the Power of Policy
You know, there’s this story a lot of us like to tell ourselves—that we’re just bystanders. Not part of the problem, not really part of the solution. It’s especially tempting to believe when the world feels overwhelming, or the headlines are packed with conflict and pain.
But here’s the thing: when it comes to racism, there’s no such thing as neutral ground. Every policy, every practice, every belief—whether we realize it or not—either helps prop up inequality or challenges it.
Let’s make this real for a moment. Picture a city council meeting, where a new housing policy is on the table. Some folks argue it’ll benefit everyone, but others warn it could force low-income families—many of them people of color—out of their homes and neighborhoods. Whatever decision gets made in that room? It’s going to shape lives for years. Supporting the policy means backing one outcome. Opposing it means backing another. There’s no neutral choice here.
And honestly, it’s not just about big policy debates. It shows up in the everyday moments, too. Like when a teacher disciplines a student more harshly because of their background, or a manager passes over a qualified candidate just because of their name. These aren’t neutral actions. They’re decisions that either reinforce—or challenge—the hierarchies already in place.
Most people don’t think of themselves as part of these systems. Maybe you’ve heard someone say, “Racism is something that happens somewhere else,” or “It’s just a few bad apples.” But the truth is, all those policies and practices? They’re built from countless individual choices, each one adding up to a much bigger pattern.
Now, it’s tempting to believe that if we just change enough hearts and minds—if people just become more tolerant—the world will get better. Sounds hopeful, right? But history tells a different story. Real progress usually starts with changing policies.
Think about when schools were desegregated. Was it because everyone suddenly became less prejudiced? Not really. It happened because the laws changed—even when a lot of folks resisted, sometimes fiercely.
That doesn’t mean attitudes don’t matter. Of course they do. But without changes in policy, good intentions alone just don’t cut it. It’s one thing to say the right things. It’s a whole lot harder to actually support the changes that would make a real difference—like fair housing laws, equal funding for schools, or reforming the criminal justice system.
The idea that we can stay neutral is a powerful myth. It lets people sidestep responsibility. But once you start to see that it’s just that—a myth—it’s hard to unsee. Every day brings a new set of choices. New chances to either support justice, or keep things the way they are.
So, the work of antiracism? It’s about making those choices on purpose. And pushing for the policies that bring us closer to real equality.
